technique: the second person — how 'you' pulls the reader into the room
lesson: Today we work on one technique. It's called the second person. That means the poem talks to "you," so the reader stands in the scene instead of watching it from outside. Look where it does this. "The latch is worn to the shape of your thumb." "You've carried this bucket till the handle knows you." "go meet it while it's still new." Each time the poem says "you" or "your," it puts the action in your hands. You feel the latch. You carry the weight. It works because the reader can't stay back. The word "you" assigns the work to the listener, so you do it in your head. Try this: write five lines about a morning task, and use "you" and "your" in each line to give the reader the job. The second time through, listen only for "you" and "your," and count how often the poem hands the work to you. Here is the poem.
poem:
The latch is worn to the shape of your thumb,
cold iron that gives with a familiar click,
and the door swings out on air that bites clean.
You've carried this bucket till the handle knows you,
its wire cutting the old groove in your palm—
a weight you've made peace with, lifted and set down
a thousand plain mornings, no ceremony to it.
The barn breathes its warm animal dark.
Something shifts in the straw and waits on you,
patient as the figures you tallied in the night,
the small accounts that square if you keep at them.
Steam lifts off the water you've hauled.

The light's already out there doing its slow work—
go meet it while it's still new.
